title: Chance, Conditioning, and Careful Updating (Prices & Consumers)
description: 50-minute first-year applied econ/social-science stats lesson on probability foundations only. Parameter vs statistic and sampling variability explicitly deferred.
course: Econ / social-science applied statistics sequence (first-year undergraduate)
audience: First-year undergraduate students in an applied econ or social-science statistics sequence
topic: Probability foundations: chance, conditional probability, Bayes-lite intuition (prices/inflation/consumer examples)
learningOutcomes: Distinguish outcomes, events, and simple probability assignments in an applied prices/consumer setting
Use conditional probability language correctly (including base-rate caution) on a short applied example
Update a simple prior with new information at an intuitive Bayes-lite level (no formal Bayes theorem derivation required)
Explain in plain language why chance models matter for reading economic numbers—without claiming sample-to-population inference yet

sections.title: Hook: a confident price claim
sections.purpose: Surface how everyday economic claims smuggle chance and uncertainty without naming them.
sections.teacherNotes: Open with a short consumer/inflation-style claim (e.g., “Most shoppers will see prices fall this month” or a store “80% of customers save”). Ask what would make the claim true/false and what “most” hides. Do not introduce parameters/samples yet.
sections.learnerTask: In one or two sentences, say what would count as evidence for or against the claim—and what still feels unclear.

sections.title: Outcomes, events, and simple chance
sections.purpose: Build a shared vocabulary for random outcomes and events using a consumer/price scenario.
sections.teacherNotes: Define outcome vs event with a concrete shopper/price example (e.g., randomly selected receipt; categories: price-up / flat / price-down on a basket). Assign simple probabilities that sum to 1. Emphasize model vs reality.
sections.learnerTask: With a partner, list the sample space for a tiny consumer scenario and assign rough probabilities that add to 1; mark one event of interest.

sections.title: Conditional probability without the trap
sections.purpose: Practice “probability given information” and flag base-rate / inverted-condition mistakes.
sections.teacherNotes: Move to P(A|B) language with a prices/consumer filter (e.g., probability a basket rose given it was mostly food; or probability a shopper is “deal-seeking” given they used a coupon). Show a 2x2 count table. Explicitly contrast P(A|B) vs P(B|A). No Bayes formula wall yet.
sections.learnerTask: Using a provided 2x2 table, compute or reason about one conditional probability and state the inverted conditional in words (do not equate them).

sections.title: Bayes-lite: updating a prior with news
sections.purpose: Show intuitive prior → evidence → revised belief without formal theorem derivation.
sections.teacherNotes: Start with a prior belief about inflation/price direction (given as simple chances). Add one piece of news (survey blip, oil move, retailer note). Walk natural frequencies or a simple tree. Keep algebra light; stress that new information revises chances, it does not certify certainty.
sections.learnerTask: Given a prior and one evidence scenario, say whether your chance of “prices up” should rise, fall, or stay put—and why in plain language.

sections.title: Exit check + bridge to next class
sections.purpose: Collect individual formative evidence on chance/conditioning; explicitly park parameter vs statistic for next meeting.
sections.teacherNotes: Individual exit ticket on outcomes/events, one conditional vs inverse, and one updating judgment. Close with a one-minute preview: next class uses chance language to talk about estimates that move across samples (parameter vs statistic)—not today.
sections.learnerTask: Individually answer three short items; optionally jot one economic headline that confuses “given” information with the reverse.

materials: One short consumer/price claim for the hook
Simple 2x2 count table (shopper type × basket price-change)
Natural-frequency or tree handout for Bayes-lite
assessmentNotes: Formative only. No consequential grading. Parameter/statistic and sampling variability are out of scope for this session by teacher decision.
assumptions: Teacher chose split intent: probability foundations only today
Defer parameter vs statistic + sampling variability to next class
No formal Bayes theorem derivation required
sourceRefs: Reconcile choice: split intent — probability only today
Domain: prices, inflation, or consumer behavior
